title: A Topological Framework for the Identification and Classification of Spanning Triplets in RNA-Protein Complexes.
abstract: Most functional RNA molecules interact with proteins. To better understand these interactions, amino acid:ribonucleotide motifs of different sizes and scales need to be classified and characterized. Although pairs of amino acids and ribonucleotides have been previously studied, structural characteristics of triplets and other higher-order spanning motifs present in RNA-protein complexes are not fully understood. This is especially significant since such motifs may act as nexus points and provide a deeper understanding of RNA-protein recognition. To advance this goal, we propose a method for the automated identification of spanning triplet motifs in the crystal structures of RNA-protein complexes using a topology-based classification and nomenclature scheme. This method is also expandable to other higher-order spanning motifs. Additionally, we investigate the frequency and composition of spanning triplet motifs present in the available crystal structures.

title: Selective transcript-protein discordance of glycolytic remodeling in human hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
abstract: Although metabolic reprogramming has attracted growing attention in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), transcriptomic and proteomic studies have yielded conflicting views on glycolytic alterations. As a master transcriptional regulator of glycolytic genes, HIF1α remains poorly characterized in human HCM tissue. We integrated four transcriptomic datasets, three proteomic datasets, and one phosphoproteomic dataset from publicly available human HCM cohorts. Glycolysis-, hypoxia-, and oxidative metabolism-related pathways were assessed by gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA). Transcript-protein concordance was evaluated by comparing the direction and magnitude of individual glycolytic enzyme changes across omics layers. Across all four transcriptomic cohorts, glycolysis-related programs were suppressed at the mRNA level (NES range: -1.1 to -1.7). HALLMARK_HYPOXIA was negatively enriched in four of five transcriptomic comparisons, and Semenza HIF1 targets showed the strongest suppression (NES = -1.99, Padj = 2.8 × 10-4). At the protein level, alterations differed by pathway. Oxidative pathways (OXPHOS, TCA cycle, FAO) showed concordant downregulation at RNA and protein levels, whereas glycolytic enzymes displayed level-specific discordance. In Garmany 2023 paired samples, 5 of 12 glycolytic enzymes showed opposite RNA and protein directions, whereas the overall RNA-protein correlation was weak and non-significant (r = -0.28, P = 0.38; n = 12) and was therefore considered descriptive. HK1 was the most prominent example of transcript-proteome decoupling, with reduced transcripts in four transcriptomic cohorts but increased protein levels across three independent proteomic platforms (Garmany TMT, Nollet LC-MS/MS, Lumish SomaScan). GSEA in Garmany 2023 demonstrated opposite enrichment patterns between transcriptome and proteome for Glycolysis (NES -1.11 vs. +1.40) and Hypoxia (NES -1.89, Padj < 0.001 vs. +1.34, ns), although proteomic enrichment did not reach FDR significance. Phosphoproteomic analysis revealed enzyme-specific rather than pathway-wide changes: HK1 (log2FC + 0.18, FDR < 10-5) and PGAM1 (+0.40, FDR = 0.02) showed increased phosphorylation, whereas ALDOA, LDHB, PKM, and PFKM showed decreased phosphorylation (all FDR < 0.01). Our study identifies a transcript-protein disconnect in glycolytic metabolism in human HCM. HIF1-associated transcriptional programs were reduced rather than activated. Oxidative pathways (OXPHOS, TCA cycle, FAO) showed coordinated downregulation across RNA and protein levels, whereas glycolysis exhibited frequent RNA-protein divergence, suggesting distinct regulatory mechanisms across metabolic pathways in HCM.

title: Machine learning for RNA-small molecule interactions: methodologies, evaluation, and future directions.
abstract: RNA is emerging as a compelling therapeutic target due to its rich structural diversity and central involvement in gene regulation, splicing, translation, and cellular signaling. Alongside advances in structural biology, computational approaches, especially machine learning and deep learning, have transformed the systematic analysis of RNA-small molecule interactions. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive survey of computational methods for RNA-small molecule interaction prediction, with a particular emphasis on three core tasks: binding site prediction, binding preference prediction, and binding pose prediction. We first summarize the data resources commonly used to support these tasks and outline molecular representations that capture RNA structural features and the chemical properties of small molecules. We then review a spectrum of computational approaches for the above three tasks, ranging from statistical methods and traditional machine learning to deep learning. We further evaluate representative methods for each task, providing insights into their respective strengths and limitations. Finally, we highlight open challenges in current research on RNA-small molecule interactions, including limited data availability, the black-box nature of the models, and the growing need for generative modeling. We discuss emerging directions such as data augmentation, model interpretability, and RNA-targeted small-molecule design as promising pathways to address these challenges and advance rational RNA-targeted drug discovery.

title: RNA Aptamer-Enabled Development of Heterobifunctionals That Chemically Induce RNA-FKBP12 Ternary Complexes.
abstract: Limitations in the druggability of challenging protein targets, coupled with recognition of the diverse roles of noncoding RNAs in cellular regulation and disease have spurred interest in RNA as a druggable macromolecule. The rapidly emerging field of RNA-targeted small-molecule therapeutics is now exploring induced proximity mechanisms in the form of RNA-targeting chimeras that recruit effector proteins to catalyze RNA decay. Inspired by "molecular glue" natural products such as rapamycin and cyclosporin A, which induce protein-protein interactions to sterically modulate protein function, we propose the new application of immunophilin recruitment to alter RNA function. Here in, we report the design and characterization of heterobifunctional molecules that induce highly cooperative RNA-FKBP12 ternary complexes and describe efforts to assess their impact on RNA metabolism. We also evaluate applications and report off-target liabilities associated with the chosen RNA ligand for our heterobifunctional series. Finally, we discuss the challenges faced and highlight opportunities for future success in the RNA space.

title: Circular RNA SMAD4 coordinates with m6A-dependent IGF2BP2 to promote gallbladder cancer development.
abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) have emerged as important regulators in tumorigenesis through microRNA sponging, protein translation and interaction with RNA-binding proteins. Here, we identified a novel circRNA termed circSMAD4 that was generated by alternative splicing from exon 2 to exon 10 and back to the beginning of exon 2 of SMAD4 pre-mRNA, constituting a 1435-nucleotide circular RNA. circSMAD4 was upregulated in gallbladder cancer (GBC) tissues and positively correlated with cancer progression. Elevated expression and tumorigenic activity of circSMAD4 mainly relied on its interaction with IGF2BP2, where m6A-binding motifs located at KH3 and KH4 of IGF2BP2 recognized and bound to the flanking intron sequences of circSMAD4. In the cytoplasm, IGF2BP2 stabilized circSMAD4 levels, and circSMAD4 in turn inhibited ubiquitination and degradation of IGF2BP2, thereby creating a positive feedback loop for both elevated expressions. Collaboration of circSMAD4 and IGF2BP2 activated JAK2/STAT3 and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) signalling. Notably, treatment of xenografted mouse models with CWI1-2, a small molecule for interruption of IGF2BP2 binding to circRNA, resulted in decreases in circSMAD4-induced tumour development. Collectively, our findings suggest that circSMAD4 cooperates with IGF2BP2 to promote tumour progression, highlighting the circSMAD4-IGF2BP2 complex as a potential therapeutic target in GBC.

title: Polyphosphate and Disordered Hfq Regions Drive DNA Compaction through Conformation-Dependent Interactions.
abstract: The RNA-binding protein Hfq and inorganic polyphosphate (polyP) were previously suggested to promote DNA compaction of AT-rich regions by forming heterochromatin-like structures, yet the underlying molecular mechanism remains unclear. Here, we combine coarse-grained and all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the interplay between Hfq, polyP, and DNA. Under physiological conditions, polyP electrostatically interacts with the distal faces of multiple Hfq hexamers, clustering them near DNA and leaving the proximal faces available to interact with the DNA minor groove via the disordered N-termini, thereby promoting compaction. While this mechanism shows limited dependence on DNA sequence, it is highly sensitive to environmental conditions. Under high-salt conditions, electrostatic interactions are screened, weakening polyP-Hfq association and limiting Hfq clustering, while stabilization of non-canonical DNA conformations exposes hydrophobic surfaces. These changes shift the mode of Hfq interaction with DNA toward its distal face and disordered C-termini, favoring hydrophobic interactions and reducing compaction. Together, our findings reveal a conformation-dependent switch in Hfq-DNA interaction modes governed by cellular conditions, providing a molecular framework for environment-responsive genome organization in bacteria.

title: The chromatin-organizer Satb1 modulates regulatory T cell activity within the tumor microenvironment.
abstract: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are essential for maintaining immune homeostasis and preventing autoimmune diseases, but are also a major cellular constituent of the tumor microenvironment (TME) that facilitates cancer progression. Identifying differences in Treg subtypes to specifically disrupt the activities of tumor-promoting Tregs, without affecting Tregs that maintain immune homeostasis remain a challenge. Here, we report that expression of the chromatin-organizer protein special AT-rich sequence binding protein 1 (Satb1), in Tregs is critical for their tumor-promoting functions in the TME, but not strictly required to suppress inflammatory T cells in autoimmune colitis. Satb1 expression differentiated between two Treg subtypes with distinct display of Treg phenotypic markers in lymphoid organs. Using transfer experiments, we discovered a context-specific switch in Satb1 protein expression between the two Treg subtypes. In mice, Treg-specific deletion of Satb1 augmented TCF-1 expression via a signaling axis involving Stat3 and the RNA-binding protein poly(C)-binding protein 1 (PCBP1), impairing the activities of tumor-infiltrating Treg cells. Simultaneous deletion of Satb1 and PCBP1 in Tregs completely restored Treg pro-tumorigenic functions and abolished the potent antitumor immune responses observed in Satb1-deficient mice. Our results reveal a key mechanism that may safely and potently enhance antitumor immunity without causing systemic autoimmune diseases.

title: Adaptive Noise Scheduling for Diffusion-based Imputation of Time-series Single-cell Data.
abstract: Accurate imputation of missing values in single-cell data remains challenging due to high dimensionality and heterogeneous structures, which can not be effectively handled by most traditional imputation methods. Diffusion-based generative models have shown strong performance by learning data distributions through progressive noising and denoising processes. However, these approaches typically rely on fixed noise schedules, and the impact of different noise scheduling strategies on model performance remains insufficiently understood. Our prior work introduced a time-varying blue noise based diffusion model for imputing missing values in time-series data and demonstrated superior performance over many existing methods. Building on this, we systematically investigate a range of noise scheduling strategies and examine how they influence both the noise injection process and overall imputation performance. Experimental results on single-cell RNA sequencing data show that the model is largely insensitive to the ordering of different noise types during injection, and that different noise schedules have limited impact on reconstruction accuracy, thereby providing greater flexibility in the design of noise schedules during model training. These findings offer a promising direction for advancing generative modeling in high-dimensional data analysis.

title: Genetically engineered RNA inducers of proximity for protein regulation.
abstract: Current genetic engineering technology that based on complementary base pairing for target recognition is a powerful tool to control protein expression at DNA or RNA levels. Nonetheless, limited research has utilized genetic strategies to directly manipulate proteins. To address this gap, we have developed a method of genetically engineered RNA inducers of proximity (GENRIP), one strategy that leverages RNA structure-dependent protein recognition to precisely regulate protein activity. GENRIP is a modular and bifunctional RNA comprising two kinds of motifs: a conserved RNA motif that recruits endogenous RNA-binding enzymes for protein modification, and a variable motif responsible for recognizing different proteins of interest (POIs). By inducing proximity between effector enzymes and POIs, GENRIP enables precise post-translational modification of POIs. Using the RNA-binding E3 ligase MEX3A and RNA-binding kinase CamK as model effectors, we have demonstrated its capability to achieve ubiquitination-mediated degradation and phosphorylation-induced activation of POI, respectively. Furthermore, GENRIP offers superior advantages in modularity, programmability, precise subcellular localization targeting, and cell-type selectivity. This approach represents a paradigm shift in genetic engineering, holding profound implications in the field of post-translational protein regulation.

title: Human senataxin uses distinct peripheral elements to unwind R-loops and act on RNA polymerase II
abstract: Persistent R-loops and paused or stalled RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) elongation complexes can threaten genome stability. Senataxin (SETX) contributes to R-loop resolution and RNAPII regulation, but their intimate connection during transcription makes the individual contributions of these activities difficult to distinguish in cells. To determine whether these activities rely on the same molecular features, we investigated the structure and biochemical properties of the SETX helicase domain (SETX-HD). Cryo-EM defines the conserved helicase core and RNA-binding channel of SETX-HD, while biochemical analyses identify distinct roles for two peripheral elements: a previously uncharacterised C-terminal RNA-binding domain (CT-RBD) and the prong subdomain. In reconstituted mammalian transcription assays, SETX-HD promotes passage beyond a defined RNAPII pause and elongation-complex dissociation on the same template. The CT-RBD stabilises RNA engagement and is required for efficient R-loop unwinding, whereas its deletion preserves both RNAPII-associated activities. Conversely, replacing the native SETX prong with its fungal Sen1 counterpart preserves R-loop unwinding but impairs both RNAPII outcomes. These reciprocal separation-of-function effects establish that a common SETX-HD RNA-translocation core depends on distinct peripheral elements for R-loop unwinding and action on mammalian RNAPII. This separation provides a direct route to determine how these activities contribute to SETX function in cells.

title: TriTower-m6Am: A triple-tower heterogeneous deep learning architecture integrating semantic, sequential, and structural information for mRNA N6,2'-O-dimethyladenosine site prediction.
abstract: N6,2'-O-dimethyladenosine (m6Am) is a cap-proximal mRNA modification deposited by PCIF1 (phosphorylated C-terminal domain (CTD)-interacting factor 1) at the first transcribed nucleotide of eukaryotic mRNAs. Knowing where m6Am sites sit would help explain how cells tune mRNA stability and translation, but current predictors typically depend on a single representation and do not jointly model multiple views of the same RNA sequence. We present TriTower-m6Am, combining semantic (RNA-FM, a pretrained RNA foundation model, with BellPooling), sequential (One-Hot BiLSTM, bidirectional long short-term memory), and structural (RGCN, a relational graph convolutional network, over the 41-nt window) representations of each RNA window. On an independent test set of 640 sequences, TriTower-m6Am reaches an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.776 and a Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.425, against DTC-m6Am's AUC = 0.765 and MCC = 0.411, using 4.4 times fewer trainable parameters; at every matched specificity between 0.40 and 0.70 it recovers 1-7 more true sites out of 320 than DTC-m6Am. The AUC-weighted voting keeps every tower's contribution readable for any individual prediction. Analyses of the graph tower delimit its benefit to the relational aggregation of local backbone adjacency over sequence-derived node features: the edge-type ablation, the node-feature ablation, and a structure-permutation control agree that the specific RNAfold-predicted fold carries no attributable signal, and a probing analysis shows that per-base base-pairing status is largely recoverable from the sequence-derived RNA-FM embeddings (AUC = 0.72 vs. 0.65 from the raw sequence), so the fold annotation is substantially redundant with the semantic representation the ensemble already receives. Combining semantic, sequential, and structural views of the same RNA sequence improves m6Am prediction beyond any single representation, and the ensemble's voting weights make each prediction auditable without a post-hoc explainer. Whether the triple-tower pattern transfers to other RNA modification prediction tasks remains to be tested in future work.

title: Decoding the phosphorylation landscape of ITPR3 across calcium signaling and regulatory networks in cancer.
abstract: ITPR3 is an endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ release channel that plays an important role in intracellular calcium signaling and has been implicated in cancer-associated cellular processes. Although several phosphorylation sites have been identified in ITPR3, the downstream regulatory networks associated with individual ITPR3 phosphosites remain poorly understood. In this study, we integratively analysed the publicly available human phosphoproteomic studies to characterize the phosphorylation landscape of ITPR3. Qualitative profiling and quantitative differential datasets were curated to identify phosphosites, followed by co-regulation analysis, functional enrichment, protein-protein interaction network analysis, upstream kinase identification and analysis of cancer-associated phosphoproteomic data using cProSite. Analysis of qualitative profiling and quantitative differential phosphoproteomic datasets identified four predominant ITPR3 phosphosites (S1832, S934, S2670, and S916) based on their recurrent detection and perturbation across independent datasets. Functional enrichment analysis revealed associations with chromatin organization, transcriptional regulation, RNA processing, cytoskeletal organization, and cellular signaling, indicating distinct regulatory patterns across ITPR3 phosphosites. Mapping of co-regulated proteins to the KEGG calcium signaling pathway identified multiple components involved in receptor-mediated signaling, IP3 generation, intracellular Ca2+ release, store-operated calcium entry, and calcium-responsive signaling. Furthermore, analysis of cancer-derived phosphoproteomic datasets showed the recurrent detection of the four predominant phosphosites across diverse cancer cell lines. Analysis using cProSite revealed distinct tumor-specific phosphorylation patterns, including significant differential phosphorylation of S1832 residue in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, S2670 in breast cancer, S934 in ovarian cancer and S916 in kidney cancer. These findings provide a comprehensive view of ITPR3 phosphorylation and highlight potential regulatory networks connecting specific ITPR3 phosphosites with calcium signaling and cancer-associated processes. Further experimental studies are needed to determine the functional role of these phosphosites and to establish their association with ITPR3-mediated calcium signaling and tumor biology.

title: Deciphering the regulatory code of RNA inosine through enzymatic precision mapping and an explainable deep learning model.
abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing is one of the most abundant RNA modifications and is involved in multiple critical biological processes; however, the precise localization of inosine and the mechanisms governing their selective editing remain incompletely understood. Integrating high-accuracy detection technologies with deep learning models can accelerate our understanding of the selective positioning and functional implications of A-to-I editing. To address these challenges, this study simultaneously developed RNA inosine sequencing by endonuclease V (EndoV) and XRN-1 (REX-seq), a highly sensitive and accurate detection method for inosine sites, and Inosine Deep Residual Enhanced Attention Model (InoDREAM), a predictive deep learning framework. REX-seq combines EndoV cleavage specificity with XRN-1 exonuclease activity to enable comprehensive A-to-I editome profiling while maintaining accurate gene expression quantification. Using this method, we identified 590,249 high-confidence inosine sites in HEK293T cells, including 84,645 novel sites. Leveraging the high-confidence A-to-I editing sites identified by REX-seq, we developed InoDREAM, which successfully predicted multiple regulatory proteins that exhibit specific binding affinity to A-to-I edited transcripts while simultaneously identifying disease-associated mutation sites and relevant cis-regulatory elements that are functionally linked to RNA editing events. These findings provide novel mechanistic insights into both the molecular regulation of RNA editing and its pathophysiological implications in disease development.

title: An anti-invasion endogenous tRNA-derived small RNA (3'-tRFAlaAGC) alleviates endometriosis by suppressing MCCC1 mediated EMT.
abstract: Endometriosis is an invasive gynecological disorder, characterized by occult ectopic endometrial growth. Nascent endogenous tRNA-derived fragments occur across various disease, yet its pathology mechanistic pathways in endometriosis remain poorly defined. Downregulated 3'-tRFAlaAGC validated from endometrial lesions and serum was demonstrated to suppress the invasion of endometriosis. Indeed, we identified that nuclear translocation of p65 mediated by MCCC1 protein was attenuated due to the occurrence of 3'-tRFAlaAGC-MCCC1 compound relying on the 383-494aa of MCCC1, a unique binding site where 3'-tRFAlaAGC directly bond to MCCC1. Hence, the activation of NF-κB pathway was inhibited, hindering the epithelial-mesenchymal transition related to the progression of endometriosis. Moreover, 3'-tRFAlaAGC alleviated lesion burden in endometriosis mice, and the precious predictive efficiency in serum through the Machine learning. Understanding the 3'-tRFAlaAGC provides a critical opportunity to dissect the mechanisms driving endometriosis progression, opening new avenues to diagnose and halt endometriosis in its tracks.

title: De novo assembly and comparative analysis of the first complete mitochondrial genome of the genus Anisomeles (Anisomeles indica).
abstract: Anisomeles indica (L.) Kuntze is an important traditional medicinal plant with diverse pharmacological activities, while no mitochondrial genome (mitogenome) has yet been reported for this species or any member of the genus, limiting our understanding of organelle genome evolution and molecular characteristics within Lamiaceae. In this study, we report the first complete mitogenome of the genus Anisomeles, which was de novo assembled and annotated for A. indica using PacBio high-fidelity (HiFi) sequencing data. The mitogenome of A. indica was assembled as a single master circular molecule with a length of 296,457 bp and a GC content of 45.42%. A total of 51 genes were identified, including 32 protein-coding genes (PCGs), three rRNA genes and 16 tRNA genes. Repeat analysis revealed relatively low repeat abundance, with 60 simple sequence repeats, 136 dispersed repeats, and 15 tandem repeats identified. Furthermore, 30 mitochondrial plastid DNA sequences were detected (24,696 bp), suggesting a substantial contribution of plastid-derived sequences to the mitogenome. RNA editing analysis predicted 444 editing sites across all mitochondrial PCGs except atp1. Phylogenetic analyses based on mitochondrial and plastid genome datasets supported a closer relationship of A. indica with Pogostemon than with Phlomoides. This study provides the first mitogenomic resource for Anisomeles and establishes a foundation for future studies of mitogenome evolution, comparative genomics, and phylogenetic relationships within Lamiaceae.

title: A homozygous C2ORF78 variant is associated with mTOR hyperactivation and neurodevelopmental defects in focal cortical dysplasia.
abstract: Focal cortical dysplasia (FCD) is a malformation of cortical brain development, yet its genetic basis remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate type II FCD in a proband with behavioral disturbances, including aggression, hyperactivity, and sleep dysfunction, but with normal early development and cognition. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the proband revealed focal cortical thickening, abnormal sulcation, and gray-white matter blurring in the left temporal lobe, consistent with FCD type II. Whole-exome sequencing identified a novel homozygous missense variant in C2ORF78 (c.1264 A > G; p.Ser422Gly), absent in population databases. The S422 residue is evolutionarily conserved, resides within a disordered, solvent-accessible region, and its substitution with glycine caused marked structural destabilization, cytosolic mislocalization, and protein aggregation. Functional studies in proband fibroblasts revealed no significant reduction of C2ORF78 protein, deregulated mTOR signaling, impaired autophagy, ER stress, and G0/G1 cell cycle arrest. Molecular dynamics simulations confirmed significant loss of protein stability and compactness in the S422G mutant. C2ORF78 interacts with RNA-binding and transcriptional regulators, and gene ontology analyses indicated roles in transcription and RNA splicing. We propose that C2ORF78 functions as a transcriptional coregulator of genes negatively regulating mTOR signaling. Mislocalization of the S422G mutant leads to a loss of nuclear function, resulting in hyperactivation of mTOR and disrupted cellular homeostasis. High expression of C2ORF78 in cerebral cortex and hippocampus supports its relevance to brain physiology. Our findings identify C2ORF78 as a novel candidate gene associated with FCD type II and highlight transcriptional dysregulation of mTOR signaling as a potential pathogenic mechanism.

title: Distinct Splicing Complexes Formed by RS2Z32 Isoforms Modulate Alternative Splicing and Flowering.
abstract: Serine/arginine (SR) splicing factors can alter downstream precursor messenger RNA (pre-mRNA) splicing patterns and influence gene expression. However, the influences of different isoforms generated by alternative splicing of SR proteins themselves on the transcription and splicing of downstream target genes in plants remain to be elucidated. Here, we demonstrate that the interaction between arginine/serine-rich zinc knuckle-containing protein 32 (RS2Z32) splicing isoforms and the Arabidopsis thaliana ortholog of human splicing factor SC35 (SC35) leads to the formation of distinct complexes, through which the recognition of splice sites within intron 3 of the transcription factor circadian clock associated 1 (CCA1) gene is regulated, ultimately resulting in an altered ratio of the CCA1 splice variants. Competitive binding of CCA1α and CCA1β to the flowering locus C (FLC) gene promoter can either promote or inhibit FLC transcription and flowering. This study elucidates the molecular mechanism by which RS2Z32 regulates FLC expression independently of its canonical splicing function, enhancing our understanding of transcriptional regulation mediated by splicing factors in plants.

title: Biomaterial Platforms for Spatiotemporal Control of mRNA Delivery in Tissue Engineering and Regenerative Medicine: Design Rules, Therapeutic Applications, and Translational Roadmap.
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) enables transient, non-integrating, and programmable protein expression, yet its regenerative potential is constrained by extracellular instability, inefficient cytosolic delivery, rapid tissue clearance, innate immune activation, and poor alignment between expression kinetics and healing programs. Biomaterial platforms address these barriers by integrating molecular protection and intracellular delivery with local retention, controlled release, biophysical support, and microenvironmental regulation. This Review critically examines nanoscale carriers, macroscale depots and scaffolds, and hierarchical nano-in-matrix and stimulus-responsive systems for spatiotemporally controlled mRNA delivery. We propose a cargo-target-timing framework linking mRNA chemistry and material properties to delivery, expression, immune responses, and tissue repair. Evidence across musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, neural, cutaneous, and visceral tissues is assessed to identify candidate expression profiles, their biological rationale, and the comparative studies needed to define therapeutic windows. Critical quality attributes, longitudinal monitoring, cross-study comparability, manufacturing, storage, dosing, safety, clinically relevant models, and regulatory positioning are evaluated. Finally, a stage-gated translational roadmap and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled, adaptive, and personalized design strategies are presented. By integrating structure-property relationships with tissue-specific therapeutic windows and product-development requirements, this Review establishes actionable principles for advancing mRNA-biomaterial systems toward regenerative products.

title: Human REXO4 is Required for Cell Cycle Progression.
abstract: Human REXO4 is a poorly characterized exonuclease that is overexpressed in human cancers. To better understand the function of REXO4 and its relationship to cellular proliferation, we have undertaken multidisciplinary approaches to characterize its cell cycle phase-dependent subcellular localization and the cis determinants required for this localization, its importance to cell cycle progression and cell viability, its protein-protein association network, and its activity. We show that the localization of REXO4 to the nucleolus in interphase depends on an N-terminal nucleolar localization sequence and that its localization to the perichromosomal layer of mitotic chromosomes is dependent on Ki67. Depletion of REXO4 leads to a G1/S cell cycle arrest, and reduced cell viability. REXO4 associates with ribosome components and other proteins involved in RNA metabolism. Overall, our results show that REXO4 is dynamically localized to distinct RNA-containing structures throughout the cell cycle, associates with RNA metabolism proteins, and is required for proper cell cycle progression and cell viability.

title: A single-residue deletion in H9N2 hemagglutinin uncouples viral burden from disease severity.
abstract: H9N2 avian influenza viruses are characterized by significant genetic diversity. Deletions within the hemagglutinin (HA) receptor-binding domain represent a notable, albeit rare, evolutionary trajectory. Here, we systematically characterized the multifaceted impact of a single-amino-acid deletion at residue 227 of HA (designated HAΔ227), a naturally occurring deletion within the 220-loop that overlaps a key antigenic epitope, using isogenic reverse genetics H9N2 viruses. Paradoxically, the HAΔ227 imposed a fitness cost and was associated with enhanced HA receptor-binding avidity, reduced apparent virion-associated NA activity, altered HA/NA functional balance, attenuated viral replication in vitro, and reduced respiratory shedding in vivo. Notably, despite this compromised replicative fitness, infection with the mutant virus was associated with an altered host immune response in chickens, characterized by elevated levels of interferon-γ (IFN-γ), interleukin-10 (IL-10), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1). These altered immune responses were associated with more severe pulmonary lesions, indicating a dissociation between disease severity and viral RNA load. Furthermore, the deletion increased the pH threshold for HA-mediated membrane fusion and substantially altered antigenic relationships. Collectively, our findings identify HA residue 227 as a functionally important site at which a single-residue deletion is associated with a phenotypic trade-off between replicative capacity and disease severity: reduced replicative fitness accompanied by altered inflammatory responses and greater tissue injury. This study highlights the potential phenotypic significance of a rare deletion in influenza virus HA and demonstrates that viral burden alone may not adequately predict disease severity.

title: Unveiling the functional landscape of A-to-I RNA editing associated with Marek's disease in chickens.
abstract: Genetic improvement of disease resistance against viral infections represents a longstanding and formidable challenge in animal breeding. The antiviral innate immune response is highly regulated at the RNA level, especially through RNA modifications. Adenosine-to-Inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing modifies the mRNA sequence. Growing evidence shows that this type of RNA editing plays a key role in mediating cellular responses to viral infections and disease resistance. However, the role of RNA editing in cellular response to MD remains unclear. In this study, we examined A-to-I editing in CD4+ T cells during Marek's disease virus (MDV) infection. By comparing MD-resistant and susceptible chicken lines, we identified 642 A-to-I RNA editing events in CD4+ T cells, most of which were located within repeat elements, particularly in the CR1 family. We observed differences in RNA editing levels and counts between the two chicken lines with different infection statuses, indicating distinct editing patterns across genetic backgrounds and infection states. Additionally, ADAR (adenosine deaminases acting on RNA) expression was correlated with RNA editing frequency. We identified 21 RNA editing sites (RESs) associated with gene expression and 42, 14, and 38 RESs with predicted effects on amino acid sequences, alternative splicing, and miRNA-target binding, respectively. A comparative analysis revealed 131 group-specific RESs and 21 RESs shared across groups. Functional enrichment analysis of genes associated with group-specific RESs highlighted several terms related to MD resistance, including the MHC class I protein complex in non-infected MD-resistant birds. Significantly, we identified two L63-specific candidate RNA editing sites, chr6:26,600,122 in MXI1 and chr16:1,716,632 in MHCY57, which were predicted to affect gga-miR-1759-3p binding and amino acid sequence, respectively. Our findings reveal the landscape of A-to-I RNA editing in CD4 ⁺ T cells during MDV infection and provide new insights into its potential association with immune regulation and MD resistance.

title: Amplified MS2 labeling reveals heterogeneous dynamics of RNA granules in the live murine brain ex vivo.
abstract: Dynamics of messenger ribonucleic acids (mRNAs) and the complexes with associated proteins (RNPs), also known as RNA granules, provide post-transcriptional control of gene expression. This regulation is crucial for cell-type diversity and activity-dependent plasticity of the mammalian central nervous system (CNS). However, elucidating the physiological significance of RNA granules has been hampered by technical difficulties to probe them in live brain. Here, we describe a novel method to visualize RNA granules in native CNS tissues of mouse. To amplify the fluorescence signal from single mRNAs incorporating MS2 stem loops, MS2 capsid protein (MCP) was conjugated with 4 tandem superfolder green fluorescent proteins (sfGFPs). Using MCP-4 × sfGFP, significantly more RNPs could be detected in the fresh acute brain slices than with MCP-GFP. Amplified MS2 signal could visualize Actb mRNAs in specific cells, either driven by promoter or via Cre-dependent expression, revealing remarkably distinct localization and movements of RNPs across different CNS cell types, including neurons and glial cells. The highly sensitive live-tissue RNA imaging could be useful for investigating the regulation of the dynamics of RNA granules in the native niche, ultimately in naive and diseased animal models.

title: msDNA: the story of a unique satellite DNA molecule in bacteria.
abstract: msDNA, or multi-copy single-stranded DNA, is a small satellite DNA observed in DNA extracts from a bacterial cell. A genetic element, usually found on the chromosome, called a retron, is responsible for producing msDNA. This small single-stranded DNA has a unique structure and is synthesized by reverse transcription from an RNA template. Retrons and msDNA are found in a large variety of different bacterial species. The msDNA molecule has also been developed into an important tool for genetic engineering and genome editing. But the biological function of this unique DNA molecule remained a mystery for decades. Recent discoveries show that a retron element can protect bacteria from infection with a virus (phage) using an abortive infection strategy. And the msDNA molecule is required for this anti-phage property. A historical perspective on this unusual DNA molecule, recent breakthroughs into its functions, and a discussion of the current and possible future directions of study are presented herein.

title: SARS-CoV-2 Nsp2 reprograms host immunity to drive pathogenic inflammation.
abstract: Despite the end of the COVID-19 pandemic, SARS-CoV-2 continues to circulate endemically, highlighting the need to better understand the viral determinants of pathogenesis. Putative functions of the non-structural protein 2 (Nsp2) have been studied in vitro, but how Nsp2 affects pathogenesis and overall viral fitness in vivo has yet to be demonstrated. Here, we generated a recombinant SARS-CoV-2 lacking Nsp2 (ΔNsp2) to investigate its role in viral replication and disease. While ΔNsp2 replicated comparably to wild-type virus in vitro and in vivo, its deletion resulted in markedly attenuated disease in K18-hACE2 mice. Wild-type virus infection induced a strong pro-inflammatory response associated with increased recruitment of monocytes and macrophages, whereas ΔNsp2 virus infection promoted a more balanced antiviral response characterized by enhanced lymphocyte and NK cell recruitment. This was accompanied by reduced pulmonary and systemic inflammation and distinct transcriptional programs, including downregulation of pathways related to RNA processing and translation. Mechanistically, CLIP-seq and proximity labeling suggest that Nsp2 interacts with host RNA and components of the translational machinery. Together, our findings identify Nsp2 as a key virulence factor that drives immunopathology by skewing host immune responses, highlighting its role as a regulator of host-pathogen interactions.IMPORTANCEThe COVID-19 pandemic has officially ended, yet the virus that causes it continues to circulate and evolve, making it important to understand what makes it cause severe disease. This study focuses on a viral protein called Nsp2 and asks what role it plays in driving illness. Using an animal model, we observed that when Nsp2 was removed from the virus, infected animals became far less sick, even though the virus itself replicated just as well. Instead of triggering the harmful, excessive inflammation typically seen with the full virus, the modified virus prompted a more balanced immune response. Further investigation revealed that Nsp2 interacts directly with the host's genetic machinery, suggesting a mechanism by which the virus hijacks immune signaling to worsen disease. These findings pinpoint Nsp2 as a driver of COVID-19 severity and a promising target for future therapies aimed at reducing inflammation rather than simply fighting the virus itself.

title: Synthetic mRNA engineering beyond prophylactic infectious disease vaccines: epigenomic and molecular reprogramming of diseased cells.
abstract: The clinical validation of mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccines in 2020-2021 accelerated the development of synthetic messenger RNA as a precision therapeutic platform beyond infectious disease prevention. Unlike gene therapy approaches that permanently modify genomic DNA, synthetic mRNA enables transient protein expression through programmable molecular engineering. This narrative review examines therapeutic applications of engineered mRNA, emphasizing its epigenomic potential. It discusses key engineering strategies, including nucleoside modifications, codon optimization, untranslated region engineering, cap chemistry, and advances in lipid nanoparticle and alternative delivery systems. Six therapeutic domains are explored: cancer immunotherapy, cardiac regeneration, monogenic diseases, genome and epigenome editing, autoimmune disease, and somatic cell reprogramming. Particular attention is given to mRNA-mediated replacement of chromatin regulators, dCas9-based epigenome editing, epigenetically derived tumor antigens, and transcription-factor-driven cellular reprogramming. The review distinguishes chemical nucleoside modifications from endogenous epitranscriptomic regulation and examines the differences between transient protein expression, heritable but reversible chromatin changes, and permanent genomic modifications. Clinical evidence, discontinued programs, and preclinical developments are critically evaluated. Despite promising advances, major challenges remain regarding delivery specificity, durability, safety, and clinical translation. Overall, synthetic mRNA represents an emerging platform for molecular and epigenetic therapeutic reprogramming beyond vaccination.

title: Exogenous Hydrogen Sulfide Promotes FAM134B-Mediated Endoplasmic Reticulum Autophagy and Inhibits Cell Aging by PERK-eIF2α and Improves Homocysteinemic Hypertensive-Induced Myocardial Fibrosis.
abstract: Hyperhomocysteinemia (HHCY) is a major cardiovascular risk factor closely associated with hypertension, myocardial fibrosis, and cardiac dysfunction; however, the underlying cellular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) has emerged as an important cardioprotective gasotransmitter, yet the role of H2S in regulating endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and ER-phagy in HHCY-related cardiac remodeling remains unknown. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the effects of exogenous H2S in a rat model of hyperhomocysteinemic hypertension and in H9c2 cells exposed to homocysteine and angiotensin II. HHCY markedly increased blood pressure, exacerbated myocardial fibrosis, and promoted cardiomyocyte senescence, accompanied by activation of ER stress signaling and suppression of ER-phagy. Administration of H2S significantly alleviated these pathological changes, as evidenced by improved hemodynamic parameters, reduced collagen deposition, and decreased expression of senescence-associated markers. Mechanistically, H2S treatment attenuated activation of the Protein Kinase RNA-like Endoplasmic Reticulum Kinase (PERK)-Eukaryotic Initiation Factor 2α (eIF2α) pathway and enhanced Family with Sequence Similarity 134, Member B (FAM134B)-dependent ER-phagy, as indicated by increased LC3-II accumulation and augmented colocalization of FAM134B with LC3. Furthermore, silencing FAM134B substantially blunted the ability of H2S to restore ER-phagy and suppress cellular senescence, supporting a critical role for FAM134B in mediating the protective effects of H2S. These findings demonstrate that exogenous H2S mitigates HHCY-induced myocardial remodeling, in part, by dampening PERK-eIF2α-associated ER stress and promoting FAM134B-mediated ER-phagy. This study provides mechanistic insight into the cardioprotective actions of H2S in hyperhomocysteinemic cardiac injury and identifies ER-phagy as a potential therapeutic target.

title: Efficient Chemical Synthesis and Enzymatic Replication of 3'-Deoxyapionucleic Acid (ApioNA): An RNA-Selective XNA with Conformational Flexibility.
abstract: Xeno-nucleic acids (XNAs) have emerged as versatile platforms due to their sugar scaffolds that enable precise chemical tuning, leading to distinct classes ranging from fully compatible systems to orthogonal systems. However, sugar-modified XNAs capable of discriminating between RNA and DNA have remained elusive. In this work, we establish 3'-deoxyapionucleic acid (ApioNA) as a structurally flexible XNA with inherent RNA-selective hybridization properties. We achieved efficient production of ApioNA oligonucleotides through an efficient asymmetric synthesis of their building blocks and systematically characterized their properties. Thermal melting analyses demonstrate that ApioNA forms moderately stable duplexes with RNA while exhibiting weak pairing with DNA and negligible self-association. Quantum mechanical calculations reveal that the apiofuranose ring populates two low-energy puckering states, and the addition of an extra methylene group enhances backbone flexibility, thereby favoring A-form geometry for RNA pairing while requiring a higher-energy state to accommodate B-form DNA. Despite its weak affinity for DNA, ApioNA supports a complete enzymatic replication cycle using commercial Therminator and Bst 3.0 polymerases with approximately 98% fidelity and is processed by native E. coli machinery in vivo. This work fills the RNA-selective niche in the XNA functional landscape and establishes sugar puckering dynamics and backbone flexibility as key design principles for programming nucleic acid pairing specificity.

title: TDP-43-related cryptic splicing reflects pathological heterogeneity in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) involves TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) dysfunction, leading to cryptic splicing, including UNC13A cryptic exon inclusion and truncated STMN2 production. Pathologically, ALS is classified into three phosphorylated TDP-43 subtypes (Types 1, 2a, and 2b) based on the distribution of neuronal and glial cytoplasmic inclusions and the density of dystrophic neurites. However, the relationship between these pathological subtypes and TDP-43-associated cryptic splicing remains unclear. This retrospective postmortem study aimed to analyze motor cortex tissue from sporadic ALS cases (Type 1, n = 12; Type 2a, n = 12; Type 2b, n = 11) with previously described subtype-specific morphological features. UNC13A cryptic RNA and truncated STMN2 RNA levels were quantified using quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR). Compared with Types 1 and 2a, Type 2b, characterized by abundant thread-, dot-, and grain-like dystrophic neurites, exhibited significantly higher levels of UNC13A cryptic RNA and truncated STMN2 RNA. Droplet digital PCR revealed a similar subtype-dependent trend and showed strong correlations with qRT-PCR measurements, providing partial support for the primary findings. UNC13A cryptic RNA and truncated STMN2 RNA levels were positively correlated (Spearman's ρ = 0.58), indicating coordinated dysregulation of multiple TDP-43-dependent splicing targets. Our results demonstrate that the burden of TDP-43-associated cryptic splicing differs across ALS pathological subtypes. Additional analyses indicated that these subtype-dependent differences were not readily accounted for by disease duration, RNA quality, normalization strategy, or semiquantitative neuronal loss scores. These findings suggest that molecular heterogeneity parallels pathological heterogeneity in ALS and provide additional insight into the biological diversity of TDP-43 proteinopathy.

title: A naturally occurring recombinant PRRSV with a JXA1-derived nsp9 fragment is associated with enhanced virulence in piglets.
abstract: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) nonstructural protein 9 (nsp9), the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, has been implicated as a critical virulence determinant of highly pathogenic PRRSV (HP-PRRSV) through reverse genetics studies with engineered chimeric viruses. However, field isolates that naturally carry such nsp9-centric recombination events-thereby serving as potential in vivo models-remain exceptionally rare. Here we report the isolation and characterization of a novel PRRSV strain TJ25928 from a farm in China experiencing a severe PRRS outbreak. TJ25928 possesses the characteristic 131-amino-acid deletion pattern of NADC30-like strains and phylogenetically belongs to Lineage 1.8. Recombination analysis revealed a distinct configuration: the backbone of TJ25928 is derived from NADC30-like strains, while a discrete fragment within the nsp9 coding region (nt 7856-8923) is derived from JXA1-like HP-PRRSV. The boundaries of this nsp9 fragment overlap substantially with the nsp9 segment previously implicated in fatal virulence in engineered chimeric viruses. In piglet challenge experiments, TJ25928 induced significant febrile response (8-12 days post-infection), pronounced growth suppression (approximately 28% reduction in total weight gain at 21 days post-infection), and 33.3% (1/3) mortality. TJ25928 represents an important example of a field isolate that naturally carries the nsp9 recombination configuration previously studied by reverse genetics, providing a valuable natural model for future investigations into the role of nsp9 in PRRSV virulence. These findings underscore the pathogenic potential of nsp9 recombination events in the field and offer a useful tool for future mechanistic studies on PRRSV virulence.

title: Tetraspanin CD81 restricts Ebola virus infection and is antagonized by glycoprotein GP and matrix protein VP40.
abstract: Viruses manipulate host cell membranes to evade antiviral immunity, prevent superinfection, and optimize their replication and spread. The Ebola virus glycoprotein GP mediates viral entry but also contributes to the subversion of host antiviral immune responses. Here, we characterize the impact of Ebola virus GP on cell surface proteins and show that it reduces cell surface availability of tetraspanins CD81, CD63, and CD9. This function is conserved among several filoviral glycoproteins but not observed for glycoproteins of other viral families. Whereas CD63 and CD9 are largely dispensable for Ebola virus replication, CD81 suppresses virus-like particle entry and viral replication. This activity might be attributed to CD81-mediated suppression of NF-κB signaling, which is induced by the Ebola virus matrix protein VP40 and transcription- and replication-competent virus-like particle (trVLP) replication. Our results further indicate that both GP, which interacts directly with CD81, and VP40, which also associates with CD81, function to reduce total and surface expression levels of CD81. CD81 is shown to reduce levels of Ebola virus RNA species, and its antibody-mediated clustering can suppress Ebola virus infection. Our study provides insights into the roles of NF-κB signaling in Ebola virus replication and immunopathogenesis, and identifies tetraspanin CD81 as a potentially druggable Ebola virus-inhibitory host factor.

title: Optimization and application of a tetracycline-inducible gene expression system in Kluyveromyces marxianus.
abstract: Kluyveromyces marxianus is a promising microbial cell factory owing to its rapid growth, thermotolerance, broad carbon-source utilization, and food-safe status. Tetracycline (Tet)-inducible systems provide powerful means for precise gene regulation in various hosts. However, Tet systems with strong induction and low leakiness remain poorly developed in K. marxianus. Here, we optimized a Tet-inducible system in K. marxianus by engineering promoter-Tet-operator architectures. The optimized rtTA-based system achieved up to 14-fold induction, exhibited a rapid response within 20 min, and functioned robustly across different temperatures and culture media. This system enabled efficient induction of genomic gene expression and supported higher heterologous protein production compared with constitutive promoters. Furthermore, we developed a TetR-based inducible guide RNA promoter derived from the native K. marxianus tRNAGly promoter, enabling low-leakage CRISPR-based gene disruption, activation, and interference. Together, these tools expand the genetic toolbox for precise gene regulation in both fundamental and industrial applications in K. marxianus. KEY POINTS: A strong, rapid and robust Tet-inducible system was optimized in K. marxianus. The system efficiently induced genomic genes and heterologous protein expression. An inducible guide RNA promoter used for low-leakage CRISPR-based gene regulation.

title: Dysregulation of mechanosensing signaling in monocytes of patients with systemic sclerosis is associated with skin inflammation.
abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a severe autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by immune dysregulation and progressive fibrosis of the skin and internal organs, resulting in substantial organ dysfunction and increased mortality. Fibrosis is driven in part by infiltration of immune cells, including monocytes that become activated within fibrotic tissue. However, how the mechanical properties of fibrotic skin regulate their function remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that increased stiffness activates human monocytes through mechanosensing. Reanalysis of single cell RNA sequencing datasets revealed that skin infiltrating monocytes exhibit heightened inflammatory signatures as compared to circulating counterparts, with further amplification in SSc. Using collagen-coated hydrogels modeling physiological and fibrotic stiffness, we show that increased stiffness enhances CD86 expression, and broadly upregulates inflammatory transcriptional programs in human monocytes. Mechanistically, stiffness-driven activation was associated with chromatin remodeling and epigenetic reprogramming, identifying the transcription factor Specificity Protein 1 (SP1) as a central regulator. CRISPR-Cas9-mediated disruption or pharmacologic inhibition of SP1 significantly attenuated stiffness- induced inflammatory gene expression, whereas we found no evidence for involvement of the canonical YAP/TAZ-TEAD axis, and pharmacological modulation of PIEZO1 neither reproduced nor blocked the response. Further, monocytes from patients with SSc displayed altered transcriptional trajectories and an exaggerated inflammatory response to high stiffness, accompanied by reduced expression of wound healing and antifibrotic programs. Together, these findings identify SP1-dependent mechanosensing as a previously unrecognized pathway controlling human monocyte activation in the skin and provide mechanistic insight into how tissue stiffness sustains inflammation in SSc.
extra: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A

title: New pathogenic ZNHIT3 variants causing fetal hydrops and lethality disrupt snoRNP assembly.
abstract: ZNHIT3 is a conserved assembly factor required for biogenesis of box C/D small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein (snoRNP) complexes, which are key players in ribosome biogenesis. Pathogenic variants in ZNHIT3 cause Progressive Encephalopathy with Edema, Hypsarrhythmia, and Optic Atrophy (PEHO) syndrome, a severe neurodevelopmental disorder typically recognized postnatally. Here, we describe two fetuses from a single family who developed isolated hydrops in the early second trimester of pregnancy, resulting in intrauterine demise. Whole-genome quartet sequencing identified two new ZNHIT3 variants, c.40T > C; p.(Cys14Arg) and c.251_254del; p.(Glu84Alafs*8), inherited from healthy parents that present as compound heterozygous alleles in both fetuses. Functional studies using a ZNHIT3 knockdown-rescue system in HEK293T cells demonstrated impaired proliferation and increased apoptosis and revealed distinct molecular consequences for the two variants. One variant produced a stable ZNHIT3 protein lacking the region required for interaction with NUFIP1 and efficient box C/D snoRNP assembly, whereas the second variant reduced ZNHIT3 protein abundance. Both variants impaired snoRNP assembly, reduced the abundance of select box C/D snoRNAs, and caused site-specific losses of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) 2'-O-methylation. These defects were accompanied by changes in ribosome biogenesis and reduced translational output. Together, our findings expand the phenotypic spectrum associated with ZNHIT3 deficiency to include severe antenatal disease and demonstrate that impaired box C/D snoRNP assembly and rRNA modification represent convergent molecular consequences of pathogenic ZNHIT3 variants.

title: Inducible and reversible in vivo protein degradation reveals T cell-intrinsic regulatory function of SHP-1.
abstract: Studying the acute, cell-intrinsic functions of signaling proteins in T cells has long been challenging. Existing constitutive or inducible gene deletion cannot overcome developmental adaptation that obscures true phenotypes. Similarly, RNA interference suffers from incomplete knockdown and off-target effects, and pharmacological inhibitors often lack selectivity. Thus, approaches allowing rapid, specific, and reversible protein depletion in defined cell populations in vivo are needed. Here, we describe an Inducible and Reversible in vivo Protein Degradation (IRIP) system in T cells by combining auxin-induced degron technology with Cre-driver-mediated, lineage-specific expression of the plant E3 ligase adaptor OsTIR1. We first validated a minimal auxin-inducible degron tag (mAID-tag) inserted into the endogenous Ptpn6 locus encoding the tyrosine phosphatase SHP-1 in murine and human T cell lines. We then generated SHP-1mAID knock-in mice and crossed them with mice carrying a floxed OsTIR1 construct in the Rosa26 locus, enabling Cre-mediated, T cell-specific, auxin-dependent SHP-1 degradation. We assessed SHP-1mAID protein degradation kinetics, specificity, reversibility, tissue restriction, and functional consequences. The mAID-tagged SHP-1 protein was expressed at wild-type levels and retained full signaling function. Auxin treatment induced complete degradation of SHP-1mAID protein restricted to cells co-expressing OsTIR1, with no loss of untagged SHP-1. Degradation was fully reversible, with SHP-1 protein restored to baseline within 2-3 hours of auxin withdrawal in vitro and 60 hours in vivo. Degradation was confined to the T cell lineage by restricting OsTIR1 expression through a T cell-specific Cre driver. Such targeting could be extended to additional cell populations using a ubiquitous Cre driver. Acute in vivo depletion of SHP-1 caused T cell hyperproliferation upon restimulation, which was reversed upon SHP-1 re-expression. These findings demonstrate that SHP-1 restrains T cell proliferation in a manner that is direct, cell-intrinsic, acute, and independent of prior developmental conditioning. Our SHP-1 protein targeting approach also resolves a long-standing uncertainty in using the motheaten mouse line or the floxed Ptpn6 locus. Our IRIP system represents a versatile and broadly adaptable platform for dissecting acute physiological roles of proteins whose constitutive loss produces complex and difficult-to-interpret phenotypes.

title: Post-Transcriptional Silencing of PHD2 by CRISPR-Cas13d Enhances Pro-Angiogenic Signaling in Human Endothelial Cells.
abstract: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) reduces tissue perfusion and causes ischemia, conditions in which hypoxia-responsive pathways have an important adaptive role. Hypoxia- inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF-1α), a central regulator of this response, is tightly controlled by prolyl hydroxylase domain protein 2 (PHD2), encoded by EGLN1. Here, we used an RNA-targeting CRISPR-Cas13d system to downregulate EGLN1 in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) under normoxia and hypoxia. A PHD2-knockdown (PHD2-KD) HUVEC line was generated by lentiviral delivery of an EGLN1-targeting RNA guide, alongside non-transduced (CTRL) and non-targeting gRNA (NTG) control lines. Molecular and functional assays assessed hypoxia-related signaling, metabolic activity, migration, and sprouting responses under normoxia and hypoxia. Western blotting confirmed a marked reduction in PHD2 protein abundance in PHD2-KD cells relative to both CTRL and NTG cells. PHD2-KD HUVECs exhibited increased VEGFA transcript levels (6.5-fold under normoxia and 5.3-fold under hypoxia) and secreted VEGF concentrations (6.6-fold and 9.4-fold, respectively), together with early increases in HIF1A transcript and HIF-1α protein levels and lower TNF-α concentrations. Functional assays showed higher metabolic activity, faster wound closure (2.0-fold under normoxia and 2.2-fold under hypoxia), and enhanced sprouting, with up to 7.2-fold more sprouts per bead and sprouts up to 2.7-fold longer than those formed by CTRL. CRISPR-Cas13d-mediated EGLN1 targeting reduced PHD2 protein abundance and was associated with higher endothelial metabolic activity, faster wound closure, enhanced sprouting behavior, and lower TNF-α secretion. CRISPR-Cas13d-mediated downregulation of EGLN1/PHD2 was associated with increased pro-angiogenic signaling and improved angiogenesis-related endothelial responses in vitro, supporting RNA-targeting strategies to modulate hypoxia-responsive pathways.

title: Licoflavone B mitigates allergic rhinitis by restraining epithelial PI3K-AKT/NF-κB NLRP3 inflammasome signaling.
abstract: Allergic rhinitis remains highly prevalent and is often incompletely controlled by current therapies, while accumulating evidence implicates epithelial PI3K-AKT/NF-κB-mediated activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in upper-airway inflammation. This study investigated whether the licorice-derived flavonoid Licoflavone B (LFB) alleviates allergic rhinitis by modulating this signaling axis. In an ovalbumin-induced murine model, allergic rhinitis-like symptoms and nasal histopathological changes were evaluated, cytokine levels were quantified by ELISA, and the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome and PI3K-AKT/NF-κB signaling was assessed by immunoblotting. Unbiased RNA sequencing followed by KEGG and GO enrichment analyses was performed to identify potential upstream pathways. The involvement of PI3K-AKT/NF-κB signaling was further explored through PI3K-AKT reactivation with IGF-1 and TLR3 stimulation with poly(I) in vivo and in primary human nasal epithelial cells (HNEpCs). Molecular docking was also conducted to explore the potential interaction between LFB and PI3K. LFB reduced sneezing and nasal scratching, partially ameliorated epithelial thickening and inflammatory-cell infiltration, and decreased mast-cell staining. LFB also reduced the levels of IL-1β, IL-6, IL-5, IL-13, and TNF-α, as well as the expression of NLRP3-inflammasome components. RNA-sequencing analysis identified PI3K-AKT signaling as one of the major enriched pathways, and immunoblotting confirmed that LFB decreased the phosphorylation of PI3K, AKT, and p65 without substantially altering their total protein levels. In HNEpCs, IGF-1 restored pathway phosphorylation and partially reinstated cytokine and inflammasome protein expression, thereby attenuating the effects of LFB. Similarly, IGF-1 or poly(I) partially diminished the symptomatic and histological improvements induced by LFB in vivo. Molecular docking positioned LFB within the PI3K catalytic pocket, providing structural plausibility for a potential LFB-PI3K interaction. Collectively, these findings indicate that LFB alleviates ovalbumin-induced allergic rhinitis-like inflammation and is associated with reduced activation of the PI3K-AKT/NF-κB/NLRP3 signaling axis in nasal tissues, HNEpCs, and stimulated mast-cell models. The partial reversal of these effects by IGF-1 or poly(I) further supports the involvement of this signaling pathway.

title: Multiple sources, shared readouts: the attribution gap in circular RNA immunotherapy for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
abstract: Therapeutic circular RNAs (circRNAs) are progressing from preclinical development to clinical evaluation, and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) may become a future indication for circRNA-based immunotherapy, potentially including first-line use. However, three focal sources-the intrinsic immunogenicity of exogenous circRNAs, the abundance of the endogenous circRNA pool, and patients' baseline interferon states-can act through different mechanisms but converge on the same readouts, including interferon output, protein yield, and immune phenotypes. Their individual contributions are therefore difficult to distinguish, complicating efforts to establish dose-response relationships. This Perspective examines this structural barrier to effect attribution and proposes strategies at three levels: product characterization and control, effect dissection, and baseline adjustment. We argue that studies of circRNA immunotherapy in ESCC and related settings should incorporate concurrent measurement of these three key, measurable sources at the design stage, with causal inference complementing association analyses to grade the reliability of attribution. Such an approach could help reduce attribution bias and provide a foundation for subsequent dose optimization and risk stratification.

title: Field-deployable seed health diagnostic assay: RT-RPA-based detection of turnip mosaic virus in mustard leaf and seed lots.
abstract: Turnip mosaic virus (TuMV) is a major constraint in mustard production, with emerging evidence of its seed-borne nature posing significant risks for long-distance dissemination and disease outbreaks. Rapid and sensitive detection methods tailored for seed health diagnostics are therefore critically needed. In the present study, a reverse transcription recombinase polymerase amplification (RT-RPA) assay targeting the coat protein (CP) gene of TuMV was optimized across multiple mustard tissues, including mature seeds. The assay was standardized at 42 °C for 25 min, and it demonstrated high analytical sensitivity, detecting viral RNA up to 10 fg dilution, particularly from crude extracts, outperforming conventional RT-PCR by 2-3 orders of magnitude. A simplified crude sap extraction using 0.1 M phosphate buffer enabled direct amplification without RNA purification, and assay compatibility with hydroxynaphthol blue (HNB) allowed visual, colorimetric detection suitable for field applications. Validation across diverse genotypes and field samples showed complete concordance of RT-RPA with RT-PCR. To establish practical seed health testing thresholds, seed pool optimization was performed using two mustard varieties differing in seed size. RT-RPA results were quantitatively validated using RT-qPCR, revealing strong agreement between qualitative and quantitative detection. Reliable detection was achieved with crude seed extracts of as few as 2-6 seeds in large-seeded genotypes and 15-25 seeds in small-seeded genotypes, highlighting the influence of seed size on detection sensitivity. This study developed and validated the first crude extract-based RT-RPA assay for detecting TuMV infection in mustard plant parts, including seed samples. It provides an ISTA (International Seed Testing Association)-compatible framework for rapid, sensitive, and field-deployable seed health diagnostics.

title: Pan-genome-based characterization of SiGRAS transcription factors and prediction of hub genes correlated with plant height in foxtail millet (Setaria italica L.).
abstract: The GRAS gene family, a class of plant-specific transcription factors, plays pivotal roles in diverse biological processes, including plant growth, development, and stress responses. Although the SiGRAS family has been previously characterized in foxtail millet, those studies were restricted to a single reference genome, overlooking critical genetic variations. To overcome the inherent limitations of gene family analysis using a single reference, we systematically investigated the SiGRAS gene family using pan-genome data generated from 110 foxtail millet accessions together with the xiaomi and Yugu1 genomes. Based on a rigorously filtered pan-genome catalog, we identified a total of 949 SiGRAS pan-genes, comprising 1 core, 20 near-core, 50 dispensable, and 878 private genes. Phylogenetic analysis classified these genes into 9 distinct subfamilies. Evolutionary analysis based on Ka/Ks ratios revealed that 8 SiGRAS genes underwent purifying selection, while SiGRAS17 and SiGRAS2 were subjected to positive selection in the majority of accessions. Notably, we observed that structural variations (SVs) significantly influenced the expression levels of SiGRAS63, and altered both conserved domains and gene structure in specific accessions. Furthermore, we identified four hub genes correlated with plant height by integrating RNA-seq data with gene co-expression regulatory network. This study lays a foundation for understanding the diversity of the SiGRAS gene family and provides a valuable resource for future function studies of SiGRAS genes in foxtail millet.

title: Beyond sequence: a half-life × localization framework for lncRNAs.
abstract: Why do long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) with similar sequences behave differently across cell types and stimuli? This opinion article argues that reading half-life together with subcellular localization provides a practical organizing dimension for lncRNA function, one that helps make sense of the context-dependent, stimulus-responsive, and tissue-specific behaviors that sequence and structure alone leave unexplained. Drawing on transcriptome-wide turnover data from RNA sequencing and related metabolic-labeling approaches, I propose a half-life × localization matrix that groups lncRNAs into four functional categories, ranging from short-lived nuclear timing encoders to long-lived cytoplasmic buffers. Representative lncRNAs illustrate these categories; several shift between categories under stimulus, with the turnover change itself serving as the regulatory output. The matrix is a lens, not a final taxonomy.

title: Diacylglycerol kinase kappa is a target of the Prader-Willi syndrome gene SNORD116.
abstract: SNORD116 is a small nucleolar RNA deficient in Prader-Willi syndrome individuals. The mechanisms by which SNORD116 conveys its effects are unknown. Here, transcriptomic analysis showed that diacylglycerol kinase kappa (Dgkk) expression was elevated in the hypothalamus of Snord116-deficient mice. In silico analyses predicted a strong RNA:RNA interaction between Snord116 and Dgkk mRNA that is fully conserved in mouse and human. In vitro experiments in human cellular models demonstrated that SNORD116 mediates 2'-O-methylation of DGKK mRNA and regulates DGKK mRNA and protein expression. In Snord116-deficient mouse neurons, increased Dgkk expression was associated with attenuated diacylglycerol-mediated activation of ERK and PKC, critical elements in neuronal signaling cascades. In mice, brain Dgkk expression peaks during late embryonic and early postnatal periods, coinciding with peak rates of neurogenesis; its expression in adults is restricted mainly to brain regions implicated in Prader-Willi syndrome pathophysiology, including the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus. Fasting acutely decreased hypothalamic Dgkk expression in wild-type mice. Increased Dgkk expression in Snord116-deficient mice could reflect derangements in this pathway that affects both brain development and cell-specific functions.

title: CRISPR mutagenesis of the MYC locus reveals a druggable ultraconserved RNA element.
abstract: Noncoding sequences comprise most of the human genome; however, their functional significance remains largely elusive. Using CRISPR tiling mutagenesis with near-PAMless, high-fidelity SpRY-Cas9, we mapped the fitness landscape of an entire human gene, the 10-kb MYC locus, at base-pair resolution. This unbiased interrogation revealed that 67% of functionally essential base pairs are noncoding. Essential noncoding base pairs are under strong constraint in the human population but show limited evolutionary conservation across species. Within this landscape, we identified an ultraconserved noncoding RNA element in the 3' untranslated region (UTR) that promotes perinuclear localization of MYC mRNA and nuclear localization of MYC protein through interaction with hnRNP L. Steric-blocking antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting this element selectively eliminate diverse MYC-dependent cancer cells and inhibit growth of patient-derived tumor organoids. Together, these findings establish noncoding sequences as major carriers of functional genetic information and identify a therapeutically actionable RNA element whose targeting disrupts MYC-driven cancer.

title: Propylene glycol supplementation modulates the luteal transcriptome in dairy cows.
abstract: Our objective was to evaluate the effects of oral propylene glycol supplementation (PG; 300 mL) on the corpus luteum (CL) transcriptome of non-pregnant, non-lactating dairy cows. Sixteen cows were synchronized for estrus and assigned to four treatments in a Latin square design: CC, water pre- and post-follicular deviation (FD); CP, water pre- and PG post-FD; PC, PG pre- and water post-FD; and PP, PG pre- and post-FD. CL samples were collected by transvaginal biopsy on D15 of the estrous cycle and D10 after subsequent ovulation, followed by RNA sequencing. The contrast D10 vs. D15 within treatment identified 1994 differentially expressed genes (DEG), with the strongest response observed in PC, followed by CC and CP. In the treatment vs. control contrast, 66 DEG were detected on D15, with the greatest response in PP, followed by CP and PC. On D10, 1206 DEG were identified, with the strongest modulation in PC, whereas CP and PP showed limited responses. PG altered the expression of genes involved in steroidogenesis, lipid metabolism, and vascular and structural support of the CL. No differences among treatments were observed in dominant follicle diameter or progesterone concentrations (P > 0.05). PG increased insulinemia within 30 min of administration, and insulin was strongly and positively correlated with CL volume (r = 0.86; r² = 0.75; P = 0.02). These findings indicate that glucogenic nutritional supplementation can modulate ovarian molecular pathways and potentially affect luteal function in dairy cows, even under positive metabolic balance conditions.

title: Dapagliflozin Ameliorates Steatohepatitis by Restoring Ca2+ Homeostasis and Hepatic Insulin Signaling.
abstract: Hepatic insulin resistance is a key driver of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and is mechanistically linked to intracellular calcium (Ca2+) dysregulation. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors provide hepatoprotection, but their direct mechanisms have been debated because hepatocyte expression of SGLT2 is limited. We hypothesized that dapagliflozin restores hepatic insulin signaling by remodeling hepatocellular Ca2+ homeostasis. HepG2 cells with induced lipotoxicity and high-fat diet (HFD)-fed C57BL/6N mice were treated with dapagliflozin. Their insulin signaling, intracellular Ca2+ dynamics, and hepatic transcriptomic profiles were assessed using confocal microscopy, immunoblotting, and RNA sequencing. Dapagliflozin was more effective than the other SGLT2 inhibitors in restoring insulin-stimulated protein kinase B (AKT) phosphorylation in HepG2 cells. Dapagliflozin attenuated cytosolic Ca2+ overload by restoring sarcoplasmic/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ ATPase (SERCA2) and plasma membrane Ca2+ ATPase (PMCA2) expression and modulating Ca2+ influx-related proteins. It also significantly ameliorated hepatic steatosis, fibrosis, and insulin resistance in the HFD-fed mice without affecting their body weight. Transcriptomic profiling confirmed a decisive shift away from fibrotic and stress-related programs toward metabolic competence, as evidenced by the stable upregulation of Atp2a2 (SERCA2). Dapagliflozin also restored physiological postprandial insulin signaling and reactivated the AKT-glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK3β)-forkhead box O3a (FOXO3A) axis. Dapagliflozin has direct hepatoprotective effects that involve reprogramming the cellular Ca2+ influx-clearance balance. This pump-channel rebalancing alleviates the Ca2+-dependent biophysical barrier to insulin signaling and provides a molecular rationale for the weight-independent therapeutic efficacy of dapagliflozin in MASH.

title: RPPH1 drives ovarian cancer cells proliferation via CDK9-c-Myc axis.
abstract: Dysregulation of the proto-oncogene c-Myc is a critical driver of ovarian cancer progression, yet the mechanisms governing its expression remain incompletely characterized. A systematic bioinformatic analysis was used to screen long non-coding RNA involved in the regulation of c-Myc transcriptional activity in ovarian cancer without MYC amplification. The functions of RPPH1 were investigated using loss-of-function and gain-of-function strategies in vitro and in vivo. The therapeutic potential of targeting this axis was evaluated using the CDK9 inhibitor Atuveciclib, alone and in combined with cisplatin, in ovarian cancer xenograft models. RPPH1 expression correlated with c-Myc activity was upregulated in ovarian cancer. High RPPH1 levels predicted worse prognosis. Mechanistically, RPPH1 directly bound CDK9, enhancing its stability and promoting phosphorylation of c-Myc at Ser62. This modification prolongs c-Myc's half-life and amplifies its transcriptional activity. Atuveciclib abrogated RPPH1-driven c-Myc stabilization and activity, while combination therapy with cisplatin synergistically suppressed RPPH1-high tumour growth in xenograft models. We delineate a non-canonical RPPH1-CDK9-c-Myc axis governing oncoprotein stabilization in ovarian cancer, providing mechanistic insights into lncRNA-mediated post-translational regulation. CDK9 represents a therapeutic target for c-Myc-driven tumours, particularly RPPH1-overexpressing, cisplatin-resistant cases without MYC amplification. The combination of cisplatin and CDK9 inhibitor offers a promising translational strategy.

title: Potential implications of targeting CSF1R in diabetic nephropathy associated fibrosis.
abstract: Diabetic nephropathy (DN) is a prevalent and serious complication of diabetes, characterized by chronic inflammation and progressive kidney damage. This study aimed to investigate the role of immune checkpoint-related genes (ICGs) in the pathogenesis of DN.
